haiku-low.q1: Only the SHA-256 token_hash is persisted. The plaintext appears only once, in the create response body.
haiku-low.q2: They cannot. Closing the dialog discards the token and nobody can show it again. They must revoke it and create a new one.
haiku-low.q3: The create request gets 409 with a reason telling them to revoke a token first. No new token is created.
haiku-low.q4: Immediately, on the next API call, because every call reads the row from Postgres and gets 401.
haiku-low.q5: They receive the same generic 401 body for every cause. The responses do not differ.
haiku-low.q6: The server hashes the presented token with SHA-256 and finds the row by unique token_hash. It is usable only if not revoked and not expired.
haiku-low.q7: A successful API call triggers it when last_used_at is null or over 1 hour old. The UPDATE repeats that condition, so racing calls cannot both write.
haiku-low.q8: Nothing: the API call is unaffected. The failure is logged without the token, and the last-used write is best effort.
haiku-low.q9: It sets revoked_at to now() on the row, which stays in the table. The list shows only active tokens, so the revoked token disappears.
haiku-low.q10: Both cases get 404. Another user's token is treated as not theirs, and an already revoked token is no longer active.
haiku-low.q11: The row exists but nobody holds the token, and it shows as Never used. The user revokes it and creates another.

sonnet.q1: It stores a SHA-256 hash of the full token (token_hash, unique index). The plaintext appears only once, in the 201 create response body (shown in a dialog); never in the database, logs or analytics.
sonnet.q2: They can't. Closing the dialog or leaving the page discards the token, and nobody (including support/engineering) can show it again. They must create a new token.
sonnet.q3: The create gets a 409 with a reason telling them to revoke a token first (revoked and expired tokens don't count toward the 10).
sonnet.q4: On the very next API call with it, which gets 401. Every call reads the row from Postgres and there is no cache.
sonnet.q5: 401 for all three, with the same generic body for every cause, so the responses do not differ.
sonnet.q6: The server SHA-256 hashes the presented token and finds the row by token_hash. It reads revoked_at, expires_at, user_id and last_used_at. The row is usable only if it exists, is not revoked and is not expired. Calls then act as that row's user.
sonnet.q7: A valid token call where last_used_at is null or older than 1 hour on the row just read triggers an UPDATE after responding, setting last_used_at = now(). The same condition is repeated in the UPDATE's where clause (id matches and last_used_at null or older than 1 hour), so a second racing call matches no row.
sonnet.q8: Nothing. The write is best effort, so the call is unaffected. The failure is logged without the token.
sonnet.q9: Revoke sets revoked_at = now() on the row, and the row stays in the table. The list returns only active tokens, so the token no longer appears.
sonnet.q10: Both get 404. The revoke only matches an active token belonging to that user, so another user's token or an already revoked or expired one returns 404.
sonnet.q11: The row exists in the database but nobody has the token. In the list it shows as "Never" used. The user revokes it and creates another.
